issues.issue: The recital describes the assets sold as "conventional, closed-end, subprime, fixed rate and adjustable rate, first and second lien mortgage loans secured by one- to four-family residences," while the Section 1 definition of "Mortgage Loan" defines the pool by reference to the description in the Prospectus Supplement and "certain other assets." A party could argue the recital's description controls or limits what was sold.

"Prospectus" is defined as the prospectus "as each may be amended or supplemented from time to time," so the document referred to is not fixed at any date, and the sentence is left incomplete in the text. Which version of the Prospectus a representation speaks to is therefore open.

"Underwriting Agreement" is defined as two documents "together" (a June 29, 2007 terms agreement and an April 13, 2006 underwriting agreement) without a priority rule between them. Section 14(a)(3), which conditions closing on sales "pursuant to the Underwriting Agreement and the Purchase Agreement," then invokes an undefined further document.

This section borrows undefined capitalized terms from the Pooling and Servicing Agreement, an instrument that is only "to be dated" June 1, 2007 and is executed after this Agreement, and it does not say what happens where a term (such as "Purchase Price") is defined in both. The PSA's "Purchase Price" definition differs from the definition in Section 1 here.

The Accredited Assignment, Assumption and Recognition Agreement is defined as being "among EMC, the Purchaser and Accredited," yet Section 10 places the back-up cure/repurchase obligation for Accredited Mortgage Loans on MSMCH and Section 11 has EMC, MSMCH and the Purchaser assign it. Which seller stands behind that agreement is left in doubt.

The definition turns on loans "originated by Accredited," but "Accredited" is nowhere defined in this Agreement (it is defined only in Exhibit C to the Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement as Accredited Home Lenders, Inc.). The class of Accredited Mortgage Loans therefore rests on an undefined term.

The Acquisition Price — the price the Purchaser must pay each seller — is left blank ("cash in an amount equal to $ i" and "equal to of"), so the consideration cannot be determined from the instrument. Section 2(c) obliges payment of an amount the document never states.

"Covered" is fixed only by reference to Appendix E of "Standard & Poor's Glossary," an external document that is undated and can change, so the content of the defined term is not ascertainable from the Agreement. Which edition of the Glossary governs is unspecified.

The single Cut-off Date Balance figure of $735,100,463.83 is applied by Section 2(a) to each Mortgage Loan Seller's loans separately, leaving it unclear whether the figure is the aggregate for both sellers or a per-seller requirement. The Agreement contains no allocation between EMC and MSMCH.

This definition designates Deutsche Bank National Trust Company as "the Custodian," while the Wells Fargo Custodial Agreement definition designates Wells Fargo as "the Custodian" in identical terms. References throughout to "the related Custodian" therefore have two candidate referents and no allocation rule.

"Due Date" is fixed by reference to the related "Scheduled Payment," a term never defined in this Agreement, while the Mortgage Loan Schedule definition and Section 10(b)(1) speak instead of the "Monthly Payment." Whether the two are the same payment is left to inference from the Pooling and Servicing Agreement.

The catch-all "or similar loan under any other applicable state, federal or local law" follows an enumeration of specific statutory labels ("high cost home," "threshold," "covered," "high risk home," "predatory"), raising an ejusdem generis question about how far the residual reaches. The qualifier "which expressly exposes assignees ... to civil or criminal liability" also may or may not modify each listed category.

Meritage Mortgage Loans are defined as a class but Meritage is omitted from the list of originators in the "MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans" definition, so no loan-level representation in Section 10(b) reaches them. The defined class is left with no operative consequence anywhere in the Agreement.

"Mortgage" is limited to instruments creating a lien on or "ownership interest in an estate in fee simple in real property," which on its face excludes leasehold and cooperative collateral that the related Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement and Pooling and Servicing Agreement contemplate. The phrase "first or second priority ownership interest in an estate in fee simple" has no settled meaning.

The Mortgage File is defined solely as "the items referred to in Exhibit 1," and Exhibit 1 lists only copies of loan documents and credit-file items, not the original Mortgage Note or Mortgage; yet Section 4(b) speaks of delivering "the items of each Mortgage File" with originals and lost-note affidavits in lieu of Mortgage Notes. What must actually be delivered cannot be squared between the two.

"Mortgage Loan" is defined as "certain" loans "as described in the Prospectus Supplement," a document outside the Agreement, rather than by reference to the Mortgage Loan Schedule that every other provision uses to identify the loans. The word "certain" gives the class no boundary within the instrument.

This 33-item definition of the Mortgage Loan Schedule cannot be squared with Section 3 and Exhibit 2, which prescribe a different 25-item list (Exhibit 2 requires the Mortgagor's name, street address, Lifetime Rate Cap, Originator, Servicer, Custodian and Appraised Value, while this list reserves those items and requires Periodic Rate Cap, Servicing Fee Rate, LPMI Fee and MIN instead). Which list the delivered Schedule had to satisfy is left open.

The definition says the rate is that borne by a Mortgage Note "as stated herein," when it must mean "as stated therein" — in the Mortgage Note; as written it points back to this Agreement, which states no rate. That mechanical error leaves the Mortgage Rate, on which the Purchase Price and Net Mortgage Rate depend, unanchored.

The enumerated list of originators excludes Accredited, Fremont, First NLC, Meritage and WMC, yet Section 10(b)(18) — sitting inside the subsection expressly limited to "MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans" — purports to make an ownership representation about Fremont, New Century, First NLC and Accredited loans. The scope of subsection (b) and this definition cannot both be given effect.

The deduction is built from a "Trustee Fee Rate," a term this Agreement never defines and which the Mortgage Loan Schedule definition does not list, while the Schedule instead calls for a "Master Servicing Fee Rate." The components of the Net Mortgage Rate therefore depend on terms drawn from the Pooling and Servicing Agreement that do not match.

The opinion may be given by "counsel for the Mortgage Loan Sellers," the very parties whose recording obligations the opinion excuses under Section 6(a), and the only check is that counsel be "reasonably acceptable to the Trustee." Neither the required content nor the standard of acceptability is specified.

"Piggyback Loan" is defined but the term appears nowhere else in the Agreement, so the definition has no operative effect. A party could argue it was meant to carry a limitation (for example on second-lien reps) that was dropped in drafting.

This Purchase Price definition differs from the "Purchase Price" defined in Section 1.01 of the Pooling and Servicing Agreement, which nets Servicing Fee, Servicing Advances and Advances payable to the purchaser without the "if such purchaser is also the servicer" condition and measures predatory-lending costs by those incurred by the Trust rather than the Purchaser. Because Section 1 imports PSA definitions and the Trustee enforces the repurchase obligation, which formula governs the repurchase amount is contestable.

A Replacement Mortgage Loan "must meet on the date of such substitution the requirements stated herein," but this Agreement states no eligibility requirements for substitute loans anywhere. The substitution remedy in Section 10 therefore rests on criteria that are missing from the instrument.

The Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement is described as being "between EMC and MSMCH," but the May 1, 2007 agreement actually attached as Exhibit 3 is between EMC Mortgage Corporation and Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Inc., a different entity from Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Holdings LLC. The identity of the counterparty whose warranties flow through cannot be squared with Exhibit 3.

"Value" is the lesser of the appraised value and "the sales price of such property at the time of origination," a component that does not exist for refinance loans, which the Mortgage Loan Schedule expressly contemplates. The formula gives no answer for that part of the pool.

This definition names Wells Fargo as "the Custodian" while the Deutsche Bank Custodial Agreement definition names Deutsche Bank National Trust Company as "the Custodian," leaving the defined term with two referents. Provisions such as Sections 4(b), 5(b) and 6(a) that speak of "the related Custodian" supply no allocation rule between them.

WMC Mortgage Loans are defined as a class, but WMC is omitted from the originators listed in the "MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans" definition, so no loan-level representation in Section 10(b) reaches them. The class is defined without any operative consequence in the Agreement.

The sale obligation is conditioned on "the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof," but Section 11 is the assignment of the Accredited and Fremont bring-down agreements and contains no conditions; the closing conditions are in Section 14. The provision cannot be squared with Sections 11 and 14 as written.

Each Mortgage Loan Seller agrees to sell loans "having an aggregate outstanding principal balance as of the Cut-off Date equal to the Cut-off Date Balance," which reads as requiring each of EMC and MSMCH separately to deliver the full $735,100,463.83. No allocation between the two sellers appears anywhere in the Agreement.

Payment is conditioned on "the conditions set forth in Section 11 hereof," but Section 11 contains no conditions and the closing conditions to the Purchaser's obligations are in Section 14(a). The cross-reference cannot be reconciled with either section.

This section defines the Mortgage Loan Schedule by the information "listed on Exhibit 2," while Section 1 separately defines the same term by a different 33-item list; the two enumerations do not match. Which controls the seller's delivery obligation is unresolved.

The clause gives the Purchaser "all scheduled payments ... due after the Cut-off Date (regardless of when actually collected) and all payments thereof," and gives the seller the same for pre-Cut-off payments; the trailing phrase "and all payments thereof" is ungrammatical and could be read to sweep in collections already allocated to the other party. Prepayments and recoveries are not addressed at all.

The delivery obligation here does not require endorsed Mortgage Notes or an unbroken chain of endorsements, while Section 2.01 of the Pooling and Servicing Agreement — the instrument this delivery is made under — requires the original Note endorsed to the Trustee with an unbroken chain and imposes different substitute-document conditions. What the sellers had to deliver to perfect the trust's title is contestable between the two.

The MERS obligation is imposed on "EMC or MSMCH, as applicable," but the expense is allocated to "EMC's own expense," so MSMCH's performance is funded by a party the sentence does not oblige. The mismatch leaves who bears the cost for MSMCH loans unresolved.

The paragraph recites that "the Master Servicer agrees that it will not" alter the MERS codes, but the Master Servicer is not a party to this Agreement under the introductory paragraph and does not sign it. Whether that covenant binds anyone is a question the instrument does not answer.

Section 6(a) directs that on a recording failure "the provisions of Section 5(c) and (d) shall apply" and Section 19 makes the Trustee's exclusive remedy "the cure, purchase or substitution obligations contained in Sections 5 and 7 hereof," but Section 5 has only subsections (a) and (b) and contains no cure, purchase or substitution obligation. The remedial machinery those sections invoke is missing from this section.

This subsection imposes obligations on the Trustee — to assign the selected Mortgage Loan and release the Mortgage File — although the Trustee is not a party to this Agreement under the introductory paragraph and does not execute it. Whether those duties are enforceable here or only under the Pooling and Servicing Agreement is left open.

The sentence beginning "each assignment of Mortgage shall be submitted for recording ... at no expense to" breaks off and resumes mid-list ("Certificates evidencing Percentage Interests aggregating not less than 25% of the Trust, (ii) the occurrence of an Event of Default"), and the enumeration labels two different items "(iv)." The triggers for mandatory recording cannot be read from the text as written.

The provision makes a recording failure "a Material Defect" and directs that "the provisions of Section 5(c) and (d) shall apply," but Section 5 has no subsections (c) or (d) and "Material Defect" is not defined in this Agreement. The consequence of the failure cannot be squared with Section 5.

The perfection fallback relies on "Section 9-305 (or comparable provision) of the applicable Uniform Commercial Code," a possession provision that had been renumbered by the revised Article 9 in effect in 2007. The parenthetical "or comparable provision" leaves which rule governs possession-based perfection to be construed.

The representation covers compliance "with the provisions hereof or thereof," but there is no second instrument referred to in this Agreement to which "thereof" could attach. The stray reference leaves the scope of the no-conflict representation uncertain.

The final clause reads "and EMC not in default with respect to any order of any court," omitting the verb, so it is not clear whether EMC represents that it is not in default or that it will not be; the parallel MSMCH provision in Section 9(f) reads "MSMCH is not in default." The omission changes what is warranted.

The representation is made about "the Mortgage Loan Seller's Information (as defined in Section 14(a) hereof)," but Section 14(a) is the list of closing conditions and defines no such term anywhere in the Agreement. The subject matter of the disclosure representation is therefore undefined.

EMC's only loan-level representation is this ownership warranty, and unlike Section 10 for MSMCH the Agreement provides no cure, repurchase or substitution remedy for its breach, while Section 19 declares the Trustee's sole remedy to be obligations "contained in Sections 5 and 7 hereof" — sections that contain none. What remedy lies against EMC for a breach of Section 8 cannot be determined from the instrument.

This representation is made by MSMCH "With respect to each Mortgage Loan," which on its face includes the EMC Mortgage Loans, although the section is headed as MSMCH's representations and Section 8 gives EMC its own (much narrower) loan-level representation. Whether MSMCH warranted the Schedule for loans EMC sold cannot be settled from the two sections together.

The representation reaches "any and all requirements of any federal, state or local law" with a list introduced by "including, without limitation," so the enumerated statutes (usury, truth-in-lending, RESPA, ECOA) give the residual no boundary. How far beyond lending-specific statutes the warranty extends is open.

"No Mortgage Loan is a High Cost Loan or Covered Loan, as applicable" leaves "as applicable" undefined — it is unclear whether it limits the warranty to loans in states where those categories exist, or is surplusage. The qualifier could materially narrow an otherwise absolute representation.

The warranty is qualified "Except as set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule," but neither the Section 1 definition of Mortgage Loan Schedule nor Exhibit 2 requires any delinquency or payment-history field in which such exceptions could be set forth. The carve-out therefore has no ascertainable content.

The insurance must be from "a generally acceptable insurer" against hazards "customarily insured against in the jurisdiction" and "acceptable to the Rating Agencies," none of which is defined or measured against any stated benchmark. Whether a given policy satisfies the warranty is left at large.

The permitted-exception list ends with the catch-all "(iv) other matters to which like properties are commonly subject which do not materially interfere with" the security, sitting against three enumerated specifics. How much that residual swallows of the absolute first/second lien warranty is a classic construction question.

The sentence warrants that the documents "have been duly and properly executed by other such related parties," which is ungrammatical and appears to be a mistake for "such related parties." As written it warrants execution by parties other than those identified.

The title policy is warranted subject only to "the exceptions contained in clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) of paragraph (4) of this Section 10," but Section 10 contains a paragraph (4) only within subsection (b), and subsection (a) has no such paragraph. The cross-reference is imprecise as to which enumeration governs.

The Mortgage is warranted to contain "customary and enforceable provisions such as to render the rights and remedies of the holder thereof adequate" for realization, without any stated measure of what is customary or adequate. Whether a given form of mortgage satisfies it is undetermined by the text.

The due-on-sale warranty is given only "[w]ith respect to each fixed rate MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loan," expressly leaving adjustable-rate loans — a large part of the pool — outside it. The expressio unius consequence for adjustable-rate loans is a question the section does not address.

The property is warranted "undamaged by waste, fire, earthquake or earth movement, windstorm, flood, tornado or other casualty so as to affect adversely the value" and to be "in good repair," terms that set no measurable threshold. Whether "other casualty" is limited to the enumerated natural events is also unresolved.

The clause warrants that the borrower did not qualify "taking into such facts as, without limitation," his credit history and ratios — a phrase from which the word "account" is missing and whose "without limitation" list has no boundary. What the originator had to consider, and against what standard, cannot be read from the sentence.

The warranty requires modifications to have been "approved by the issuer of the title insurer," a garbled phrase (the insurer has no issuer) that leaves whose approval was needed unclear. It also requires modification terms to be "reflected in the Mortgage Loan Schedule," which has no field for them.

This ownership warranty is given as to Fremont, New Century, First NLC and Accredited loans, but it sits within subsection (b), whose chapeau limits it to "MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans," a defined class that excludes Fremont, First NLC and Accredited originations. The two cannot both be given effect.

The appraisal is warranted to have been made by a Qualified Appraiser "duly appointed by MSMCH," yet the MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans are by definition loans originated by third-party originators such as Aames, Aegis and Option One, not by MSMCH. Who had to appoint the appraiser cannot be squared with the definition.

The warranty turns on "LTV," a term this Agreement never defines; the related Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement defines "Loan-to-Value Ratio" and "CLTV" as separate measures with different denominators. Whether the 100% cap is tested by LTV or CLTV for second liens is left open.

MSMCH warrants that each prepayment penalty "will be enforced by MSMCH for the benefit of the Purchaser," although under the Pooling and Servicing Agreement collection and enforcement lie with the Servicers and Master Servicer, not MSMCH. Who must enforce, and what breach follows from non-collection, is unresolved between the documents.

The paragraph provides that on substitution the Section 10 representations "shall be deemed to be made by the related Mortgage Loan Seller," which would impose MSMCH's loan-level warranties on EMC even though Section 8 gives EMC only an ownership warranty. The two provisions cannot be reconciled as to what EMC warrants.

This paragraph makes cure, purchase or substitution the "sole and exclusive remedy" of the Purchaser, Trustee and Certificateholders, while Section 19 declares the Trustee's sole and exclusive remedy to be "the cure, purchase or substitution obligations contained in Sections 5 and 7 hereof" — sections that contain no such obligations. Which provision defines the Trustee's remedy is contestable.

The clause says that "within 90 days from the date of discovery ... MSMCH will, (i) cure ... (ii) purchase ... or (iii) ... substitute," without saying who elects among the three or whether notice and expiry of the 90 days is a condition precedent to suit. It also limits the remedy "with respect to the MSMCH Represented Mortgage Loans," leaving breaches of the Section 10(a) representations made as to every Mortgage Loan without any stated remedy.

The backstop is triggered by breach of "a representation or warranty set forth in this Section 10 made by Accredited," but Accredited makes no representation in Section 10 — its warranties live in the Accredited Assignment, Assumption and Recognition Agreement, which Exhibit 8 does not reproduce ("Please See Tab #13"). What breach triggers MSMCH's obligation cannot be determined from the instrument.

The clause provides that a cause of action "shall accrue" only upon discovery of the breach and MSMCH's failure to cure, purchase or substitute, which conflicts with the rule that a warranty claim accrues at closing and squarely raises whether the parties could postpone accrual by contract. It also does not say what happens where MSMCH neither discovers nor is given notice.

Sections 2(a), 2(c) and 20 all refer to "the conditions set forth in Section 11" and to "Section 11(a)" and "Section 11(b)," but this Section 11 contains no conditions at all — only the assignment of two agreements, lettered (a) and (b). The conditions those sections invoke cannot be found here.

The exception is for defaults affecting the transactions "contemplated hereby or thereby," but no second instrument is referred to in the sentence for "thereby" to attach to. The stray reference leaves the reach of the representation uncertain.

The condition requires that no event have occurred which would constitute a default "under this Agreement or the Pooling and Servicing Agreement," an agreement dated as of June 1, 2007 but executed at or after this closing. Testing default under an unexecuted instrument as of the Closing Date cannot be squared with the recital describing the PSA as one "to be dated."

Item (iv) requires opinions of counsel "otherwise in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to the Purchaser," where the stray "otherwise" indicates that the required subject matter of the opinions has dropped out of the text. What the opinions must cover is therefore unstated.

The condition refers to sales "pursuant to the Underwriting Agreement and the Purchase Agreement," but "the Purchase Agreement" is a term nowhere defined in this Agreement, which calls itself "this Agreement." Which instrument must have governed the sale to Bear Stearns is left unidentified.

Fees and expenses are payable "as previously agreed," incorporating an unidentified prior understanding, while Section 29 declares this Agreement the entire agreement and supersedes "all prior and contemporaneous agreements ... oral or written." The two provisions cannot both be given effect as to the fee arrangement.

The section recites only what Deloitte & Touche LLP "will review" and "will also confirm," imposing no obligation on any party to procure or deliver the comfort letters except a general duty to cooperate. Whether any party promised that the letters would be delivered is not answered by the text.

The facsimile number given for EMC, "241-626-4714," is not a valid number and does not match the (469) 759-4714 number given for the same Lewisville address in the attached Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement. Effective notice by the permitted facsimile route is therefore uncertain.

The section makes the Trustee's sole and exclusive remedy "the cure, purchase or substitution obligations contained in Sections 5 and 7 hereof," but Section 5 (Examination of Mortgage Files) and Section 7 (representations concerning EMC) contain no cure, purchase or substitution obligation — those appear only in Section 10 as to MSMCH. What remedy the Trustee has cannot be determined from the cross-reference.

The proviso preserves for the Purchaser "the benefits set forth in Sections 12, 14 and 18 hereto," but Section 12 is marked "[Reserved]" and Sections 14 and 18 (closing conditions and notices) confer no post-assignment benefits. The reservation refers to benefits the Agreement does not contain.

Termination rights are keyed to "the conditions ... set forth under Section 11(a)" and "Section 11(b)," but the closing conditions are in Sections 14(a) and 14(b); Section 11 merely assigns two agreements. The termination right cannot be exercised by reference to the section named.

This survival clause keeps "all representations, warranties and agreements" operative and in full force, which sits awkwardly with the Section 10 paragraph making cure, purchase or substitution the sole and exclusive remedy and with the accrual clause conditioning any cause of action on failure to cure. Whether survival preserves any claim beyond the repurchase protocol is open.

The clause says that where a provision is prohibited or invalid "this Agreement shall be ineffective only to such extent," making the Agreement rather than the offending provision the thing rendered ineffective. The sentence does not say the invalid provision is severed.

Amendment requires "the prior written consent of each party," but Section 19 provides that on assignment the Trustee "shall succeed to the applicable rights and obligations of the Purchaser hereunder," leaving unclear whether the Trustee's consent is thereafter required. Who counts as a "party" after assignment is unaddressed.

This section obliges each party to take actions and execute "any amendments hereto which may be required by either Rating Agency," while Section 24 provides the Agreement "cannot be amended or modified in any manner without the prior written consent of each party." Whether a Rating Agency demand can compel an amendment over a party's objection is the conflict.

The Agreement is made enforceable by Bear Stearns "to the extent specified in Section 14 hereof," but Section 14 (Conditions to Closing) specifies nothing for Bear Stearns; the only benefits running to Bear Stearns appear in Sections 5(a) and 16. The extent of Bear Stearns's third-party rights cannot be determined from the cross-reference.

The entire-agreement clause supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements on the subject matter, yet Section 15 makes fees payable "as previously agreed" and Section 1 imports definitions from the Pooling and Servicing Agreement. Whether those extrinsic arrangements survive the merger clause is contestable.

Exhibit 1 requires only "Copies of the Mortgage Loan Documents" and credit-file items, to be "delivered to the Purchaser or its designee," while Section 4(b) requires the items of each Mortgage File to be delivered to the Trustee or Custodian with originals and lost-note affidavits in lieu of Mortgage Notes. What had to be delivered, in what form and to whom, cannot be squared between the two.

This Exhibit 2 list of Schedule information conflicts with the 33-item Mortgage Loan Schedule definition in Section 1 — it requires the Mortgagor's name, street address, occupancy code, last payment date, Lifetime Rate Cap, Index code, Originator, Servicer, Custodian, Purchase Date and Appraised Value, which Section 1 reserves or omits, and omits the Servicing Fee Rate, LPMI Fee, MIN and Prepayment Charge that Section 1 requires. Which list the Schedule had to satisfy is unresolved.

The aggregate line requires "the total of each of the amounts described under (0) above," but item (o) is the Interest Rate Adjustment Date, which is a date and cannot be totaled; the intended reference is evidently item (n), the principal balances. The mechanical error leaves the required aggregate unidentified.

This agreement is between EMC and Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Inc., a New York corporation, whereas the Section 1 definition of "Underlying EMC Purchase Agreement" in the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement describes the May 1, 2007 agreement as being "between EMC and MSMCH" — Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Holdings LLC. Which Morgan Stanley entity gave the underlying warranties cannot be squared between the two.

"Accepted Servicing Practices" is defined by reference to "accepted mortgage servicing practices of prudent mortgage lending institutions," a circular and unmeasured standard, and the defined term is not used in any operative provision of this agreement. Its content and effect are both indeterminate.

"Appraised Value" is simply the value stated in an appraisal, with no lesser-of-appraisal-or-sales-price test, while the CLTV definition qualifies it as "the Appraised Value as determined pursuant to the Underwriting Guidelines" and the Loan-to-Value Ratio definition imposes a lesser-of test. The three cannot be applied consistently to the same property.

The Assignment of Mortgage must be both "in recordable form and in blank" and yet "sufficient ... to give record notice of the sale of the Mortgage to the Purchaser," requirements that pull against each other since a blank assignment names no assignee. Exhibit A-1(e) makes the choice depend on whether it is to be recorded, which this definition does not.

The Closing Date is May 31, 2007, one day before the June 1, 2007 Cut-off Date by reference to which Section 4 computes the Purchase Price and the Stated Principal Balance. A closing that precedes the balance measurement date cannot be worked through as written.

The denominator is "the Appraised Value as determined pursuant to the Underwriting Guidelines," but "Underwriting Guidelines" is a capitalized term that this agreement never defines. Whose guidelines determine the value, and therefore the ratio, is unstated.

"Covered" is fixed only by Appendix E of "Standard & Poor's Glossary," an undated external document that may be revised, so the category cannot be determined from the agreement itself. Which version of the Glossary governs is unspecified.

The Custodian is "the custodian specified on the Mortgage Loan Schedule attached as Exhibit B hereto," but Exhibit B as attached states only "Provided Upon Request" and contains no such designation. The identity of the Custodian, on whom Sections 5 and 6.03 depend, is not ascertainable from the instrument.

The Cut-off Date of June 1, 2007 falls after the May 31, 2007 Closing Date, although Section 4 fixes the Purchase Price by the Stated Principal Balance "after application of payments of principal due or received on or before the Cut-off Date." The two dates cannot be reconciled as a sequence.

The definition reads "repurchased or to be repurchase or replaced," a grammatical error that obscures whether a loan becomes a Deleted Mortgage Loan on repurchase, on becoming subject to repurchase, or on substitution. The trigger point matters for the substitution mechanics in Subsection 8.02.

The definition refers to "the FHA Regulations," a capitalized term never defined in this agreement. The circumstances in which the Commissioner or Secretary is included in "FHA" therefore rest on an undefined reference.

The definition of Co-op Loan breaks off mid-sentence ("secured by the pledge of stock allocated toa"), so the collateral it describes is incomplete on the face of the document. What qualifies as a Co-op Loan — which drives the Mortgage, Mortgaged Property and title-insurance provisions — cannot be read from the text.

"Fixed Rate Mortgage Loan" is defined as "a fixed rate mortgage loan purchased pursuant to this Agreement," a circular definition that supplies no criterion. Loans with fixed-then-adjusting rates are not addressed.

"FPD" is defined as first payment default provisions "as described in Subsection 8.03," but Subsection 8.03 describes no such provisions; it simply refers to the FPD provisions of the related Prior Purchase Agreements. The content of the defined term is located in documents outside this agreement.

The list runs "... NC Capital Corporation and Option One Mortgage Corporation, Option One Owner Trust 2001-1A, ...", so the conjunction placement leaves it unclear whether the Option One Owner Trusts are additional named sellers within Group 1 or a gloss on Option One. The group definition drives which loans get the Part A representations in Exhibit F.

The catch-all "or similar loan under any other applicable state, federal or local law" follows enumerated statutory labels, raising an ejusdem generis question about the reach of the residual. It is also unclear whether the assignee-liability qualifier limits every listed category or only the residual.

The date is that "specified in the related Mortgage Note and the Mortgage Loan Schedule," with no rule for the case in which the Note and the Schedule disagree. The Schedule itself is not attached, being "Provided Upon Request."

The Letter Agreement, which fixes the Purchase Price Percentage and is a required closing document under Section 10, is between Morgan Stanley & Co. Incorporated and Bear, Stearns & Co. Inc. — neither of them a party to this agreement. The price term therefore depends on a contract the contracting parties did not make.

The first sentence defines the Lifetime Rate Cap as a provision of the Mortgage Note, while the second imposes a substantive cap measured by "the amount per annum set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule," so the Note and the Schedule can produce different maximum rates. Which governs is not stated.

The denominator is the lesser of the Appraised Value and, "if the Mortgage Loan was made to finance the acquisition," the purchase price — leaving no second element for refinance loans — while the numerator uses the Cut-off Date balance even though the representations speak of the ratio "at origination." The ratio yields different answers depending on which reading is taken.

The MERS Procedure Manual is incorporated "as it may be amended, supplemented or otherwise modified from time to time," so obligations measured by it can change without the parties' assent. The definition also uses a title ("MERS Procedures Manual") different from the term defined.

"Mortgage" is defined as the instrument "which creates a first lien on the Mortgaged Property," yet the agreement separately defines Second Lien Loan and Exhibit F warrants second liens on second lien loans. The definition cannot be given effect for the second-lien part of the pool.

The Mortgage File includes the Exhibit A-2 items "(to the extent in the possession of the applicable Servicer)," while Exhibit A-2 itself qualifies the same list "(to the extent in the possession of the applicable Seller)." Whose possession limits the delivery obligation cannot be determined from the two together.

"Mortgage Interest Rate Cap" (the limit on each adjustment) overlaps with the separately defined "Periodic Rate Cap," and the Qualified Substitute Mortgage Loan definition requires substitutes of the same type "with same Mortgage Interest Rate Caps." Which of the two defined caps must match is unresolved.

The Mortgage Loan Schedule is stated to be "attached as Exhibit B hereto," but Exhibit B as attached says only "Provided Upon Request," so the loan-by-loan data that the definition, the Custodian definition and Section 4's price calculation depend on is not in the instrument. What was actually agreed as the Schedule is left to extrinsic proof.

"Originator" is defined only "[a]s defined in the Recitals," where it means the "various originators" from which the Seller bought loans, so an operative defined term is supplied by a recital rather than by the body. Exhibit C names only six such originators, which does not obviously match "various originators."

The definition reads "the absolute maximum amount by which the Mortgage Interest Rate there may increase or decrease," a garbled phrase, and it duplicates the separately defined "Mortgage Interest Rate Cap." It also fixes the cap by what is "set forth as such on the Mortgage Loan Schedule" with no rule if the Note differs.

The "applicable" Prior Purchase Agreement is to be found on Exhibit C, but Exhibit C lists several successive amended and restated agreements per originator against multiple purchase dates without stating which governs a given loan. Which agreement's warranties were assigned for a particular loan is not determinable from the exhibit.

The Purchase Price Percentage — the operative price term, and a component of the Repurchase Price — is fixed only by the Letter Agreement between Morgan Stanley & Co. Incorporated and Bear, Stearns & Co. Inc., neither of which is a party to this agreement and which is not attached. The price cannot be determined from the instrument.

A Qualified Appraiser must have been "duly appointed by the Seller," although the recitals state that the Seller purchased the Mortgage Loans from various Originators who arranged the appraisals at origination. The requirement cannot be satisfied as written for loans the Seller did not originate.

"Qualified Correspondent" is defined at length, together with "Designated Guidelines," but neither term is used in any operative provision or in Exhibit F. The definition has no work to do, raising the question whether a qualification meant to condition the representations was dropped.

Clause (ii) requires a Mortgage Interest Rate "not less than and not more than 1% greater than" that of the Deleted Mortgage Loan, an incomplete comparative that omits what the rate must not be less than, and clause (iii) uses the same construction for term to maturity. The eligibility test cannot be applied as written.

The definition allows successors "designated by the Purchasers," a plural referring to a party this agreement defines in the singular, leaving unclear who may designate a replacement agency. The term is also used only in Exhibit F's hazard-insurance representation, in the plural form "Rating Agencies."

Regulation AB is incorporated "as amended from time to time" and as subject to whatever clarification the Commission or its staff "may" later provide, so the Seller's Section 12 disclosure obligations can change after signing. The content of the obligation is not fixed by the instrument.

"Representations and Warranties" is defined in Subsection 8.02 to mean the representations of the related Originator under the Prior Purchase Agreements, yet the cure and repurchase paragraphs of Subsection 8.02 use the same defined term in a way that appears to reach the Seller's own Exhibit F representations. Which set of warranties triggers the repurchase machinery turns on this definition.

The Repurchase Price is built on the "Purchase Price Percentage," which is fixed only in a Letter Agreement between two non-parties and is not attached, so the repurchase amount cannot be computed from this instrument. It also differs from the 100% par-plus-interest "Purchase Price" the securitization documents use for the same loans.

The list ends "(vi) a Manufactured Home, none of which is a mobile home," and it is unclear whether the qualifier attaches only to Manufactured Homes or to all six categories. The distinction between a manufactured home and a mobile home is also left undefined.

"Second Lien Loan" presupposes a Mortgage creating a second lien, but the "Mortgage" definition in this same section describes an instrument "which creates a first lien on the Mortgaged Property." The two definitions cannot both be given effect.

The Servicer is "the Servicer set forth on Exhibit B," but Exhibit B as attached says only "Provided Upon Request," while Section 7 speaks of the Servicing Agreements "set forth on Exhibit C." Which exhibit identifies the servicer for a given loan is unresolved.

Servicing Rights are reserved to the Seller under Subsection 6.01 and include "any and all documents, files, records, servicing files ... or other information pertaining to the Mortgage Loans," which overlaps the Mortgage Files that Subsection 6.01 conveys to the Purchaser. Which party is entitled to the overlapping files cannot be settled from the two provisions.

Clause (i) is "the principal balance of such Mortgage Loan at the Cut-off Date after giving effect to payments of principal due on or before such date," where "such date" could mean the Cut-off Date or the date of determination in the opening words. The choice changes the balance on which the Purchase Price and Repurchase Price are computed.

The quantity purchased is an aggregate Stated Principal Balance "in an amount set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule," but the Schedule attached as Exhibit B states only "Provided Upon Request." How much was agreed to be bought cannot be determined from the instrument.

The Schedule must be delivered at least two Business Days before the May 31, 2007 Closing Date, yet the Schedule's own definition requires balances, rates and payment data "as of the Cut-off Date" of June 1, 2007 — data that cannot exist when delivery is due. The two dates cannot be worked together.

The price is the Purchase Price Percentage times the aggregate Stated Principal Balance "after application of payments of principal due or received on or before the Cut-off Date," although the Stated Principal Balance definition already gives effect to principal due on or before that date. Read literally the deduction is taken twice.

The Purchaser takes principal from the Cut-off Date (June 1, 2007) but interest only "from and after the Closing Date" (May 31, 2007), so the two entitlements are measured from different dates, and the same section's price is computed as of the Cut-off Date. Who owns interest accruing between the two dates is left unresolved.

The examination right runs through "the applicable Custodian (as set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule attached as Exhibit B hereto)," but Exhibit B is not attached in substance ("Provided Upon Request") and identifies no custodian. The mechanics of the pre-closing review cannot be carried out from the document.

This subsection assigns the Prior Purchase Agreements "except with respect to the Group 1 Mortgage Loans," while Subsection 8.02 states flatly that the Purchaser "shall be the assignee of the representations and warranties of the related Originator ... as described in Subsection 6.01" without that carve-out. Whether the Purchaser holds Originator warranties for Group 1 loans is contestable.

Record title is to remain "in the name of the Seller or an Affiliate of the Seller" while ownership is "vested solely in the Purchaser," and all funds received after the Cut-off Date belong to the Purchaser even though Section 4 gives the Purchaser interest only from the Closing Date. The provisions pull in different directions on both title and cash.

The paragraph breaks off mid-sentence ("and a asa a sale of assets 0 on the"), so the corresponding accounting and tax treatment required of the Seller is missing from the text. What the parties agreed about the Seller's books cannot be read from the provision.

Subsection 8.02 requires substitute loans to be delivered "with the Mortgage Note endorsed as required by Subsection 6.03," but this subsection imposes no endorsement requirement at all — endorsement appears only in Exhibit A-1. The delivery standard invoked elsewhere is absent here.

The loans are said to be sold "on a servicing retained basis," yet Subsection 6.01 reserves the Servicing Rights to the Seller while the next paragraph of this section assigns each Servicing Agreement to the Purchaser and has the Servicer service "for the Purchaser." Who holds the servicing after closing cannot be squared across the three provisions.

The servicing arrangements are to be "as set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule attached as Exhibit C hereto," but the Mortgage Loan Schedule is Exhibit B and Exhibit C contains the Prior Purchase Agreements and Servicing Agreements tables. The cross-reference points to the wrong exhibit.

Servicing of the Non-transferred Loans is to move to Saxon on "the related Servicing Transfer Dates set forth on Exhibit E," two of which (July 2, 2007) fall after the Closing Date and after the loans have been on-sold, and the exhibit's stated amounts exceed the pool being sold. How the transfer obligation operates post-sale is unaddressed.

The sentence contains the phrase "is required" twice ("No consent ... is required for the transactions ... having jurisdiction over the Seller is required or, if required ..."), leaving the representation ungrammatical. Whether it warrants that no consent is needed, or only that any needed consent has been obtained, is unclear.

The no-conflicts representation is limited to breaches of "the Seller's charter or by-laws," omitting any warranty against conflict with law or with other agreements binding the Seller. Whether that omission was deliberate limits what the Purchaser can claim.

The representation is that the Seller "does not believe, nor does it have any reason or cause to believe, that it cannot perform," a purely subjective formulation with no objective benchmark. What state of knowledge breaches it is not ascertainable.

This paragraph states that the Purchaser is assignee of the Originators' representations "as described in Subsection 6.01," but Subsection 6.01 excludes the Group 1 Mortgage Loans from the assignment of the Prior Purchase Agreements. It also fixes the defined term "Representations and Warranties" as the Originators' warranties only, which the later remedy paragraphs appear to use more broadly.

The Seller's own Exhibit F warranties are made here, but the repurchase machinery in the following paragraphs is triggered by breach of a "Representation and Warranty" — a term the preceding paragraph defines as the Originators' warranties under the Prior Purchase Agreements. Whether the Seller's Exhibit F warranties carry the repurchase remedy is therefore in doubt.

The trigger is the breach of "a Representation and Warranty," the defined term meaning the Originators' warranties under the Prior Purchase Agreements, even though condition (2) then addresses what the Originator has failed to do and Exhibit F contains the Seller's own warranties. Which warranties set the 120-day clock running cannot be settled from the paragraph.

The paragraph says that "within 120 days ... the Seller shall take such actions as described in the following paragraph," while the following paragraph independently allows 120 days from discovery or notice to cure before repurchase is required. Whether the 120 days is one period or two consecutive ones is unclear.

The substitution alternative applies where the Seller learns of the breach "within 180 days of the Closing Date" but requires the substitution to be "effected not later than 180 days after the Closing Date," so a breach discovered near day 180 leaves no time to substitute, and the 120-day cure period in the second sentence can outrun the substitution window. The remedies cannot be sequenced as written.

Substitution must be effected by delivering "the documents required by Subsection 6.03, with the Mortgage Note endorsed as required by Subsection 6.03," but Subsection 6.03 requires only custodial certifications and imposes no endorsement requirement, which appears instead in Exhibit A-1. The delivery obligation invokes a standard the cited subsection does not contain.

This paragraph declares cure, substitution, repurchase and indemnity to be "the sole remedies of the Purchaser" for warranty breaches, while Section 13 provides that all of the Purchaser's rights and remedies "are distinct from, and cumulative with, any other rights or remedies under this Agreement or afforded by law or equity." The two cannot both be given effect.

The indemnity is available only "provided the Mortgage Loans are not the subject of a Reconstitution," yet Section 12 contemplates that the Purchaser will securitize these very loans. On the transaction the parties planned, the indemnity limb of the remedy disappears.

The clause postpones accrual of any cause of action until discovery of the breach and the Seller's failure to cure or repurchase, which conflicts with the rule that a warranty claim accrues when the warranty is made and squarely raises whether accrual can be contracted around. It also reverses the natural pairing by speaking of "notice thereof by the Seller or the Servicer to the Purchaser."

The Seller's first-payment-default obligation is defined entirely by reference to "the FPD provisions under the related Prior Purchase Agreement," and the defined term FPD in turn points back to this subsection, so the content of the obligation lies wholly outside the agreement. Which originator agreement governs a given loan is itself set only by Exhibit C.

The trigger turns on the loan's "paid-through date (as set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule)," but the Mortgage Loan Schedule definition contains no paid-through date field — only "the last payment date on which a payment was actually applied." The repurchase event is keyed to data the Schedule is not required to carry.

The section repeatedly contemplates "each Closing Date" and multiple closings, while "Closing Date" is defined as the single date May 31, 2007 and Section 2 contemplates one purchase. Whether further closings were possible is unresolved between the two.

The condition requires information sufficient to compute the Purchase Price "(including accrued interest)," but the Section 4 Purchase Price formula is percentage times Stated Principal Balance and contains no accrued-interest component. The two cannot be reconciled on what the Purchaser owed at closing.

The condition's text is broken by the stray insertion of "(iv) (v)" mid-sentence, so the requirement that closing documents be "in such forms as are agreed upon and acceptable to the Purchaser" runs into the following items. The clause boundaries cannot be read from the document.

This condition makes "all other terms and conditions of this Agreement (unless waived)" a condition of closing, without materiality and without saying who may waive or in what form. It converts every obligation, including post-closing ones, into a closing condition.

The list of Closing Documents is numbered only as far as "1." and the remaining four items are unnumbered, so it is unclear whether they are separate documents or subparts of the first. It also requires a "fully executed original" of the Letter Agreement, a contract between two entities that are not parties here.

The Seller pays recordation fees for the Mortgage and Assignment of Mortgage here, while Section 24 makes recordation an expense of the Seller only when "necessary under applicable law or requested by the Purchaser," and the Mortgage Loan Purchase Agreement puts all recording fees on EMC. Which cost allocation governs a given recording is not clear across the documents.

This paragraph limits the Purchaser to one Reconstitution, while Section 18 states that "[t]he Purchaser shall be limited to three (3) assignments or transfers with respect to the Mortgage Loans and this Agreement as described in Section 12." The two limits cannot both be applied.

The Seller must use "reasonable best efforts" to supply information and must execute any Reconstitution Agreement "reasonably required by the Purchaser and reasonably acceptable to the Seller," a standard that gives the Seller a veto measured only by its own reasonableness. What cooperation is actually owed is left undetermined.

The Seller's backstop applies to breaches of "a Representation and Warranty" by an Originator under the Prior Purchase Agreements "assigned to the Purchaser pursuant to Subsection 6.01," but Subsection 6.01 excludes the Group 1 Mortgage Loans from that assignment. Whether the backstop reaches Group 1 loans cannot be settled from the two provisions.

The indemnity runs to persons who control the indemnified parties "within the meaning of Section 15 of the Securities Act and Section 20 of the Exchange Act," but neither "Securities Act" nor "Exchange Act" is a defined term in this agreement. The class of indemnitees is fixed by references the document does not supply.

This section declares all of the Purchaser's rights and remedies "cumulative with" any other remedies at law or equity, while the closing sentence of Subsection 8.02 makes cure, substitution, repurchase and indemnity "the sole remedies of the Purchaser" for warranty breaches. Which controls a warranty claim is the conflict.

The notice block labels only item (ii) "if to the Purchaser" and leaves item (i) unlabelled, and notice is "duly given if mailed" but deemed received only when delivered, so giving and receiving are measured differently. When a notice takes effect is not clear from the section.

This section limits the Purchaser to "three (3) assignments or transfers with respect to the Mortgage Loans and this Agreement as described in Section 12," while Section 12 expressly limits the Purchaser to one Reconstitution. The two caps on transfers cannot be reconciled.

The exhibits are made "an integral part of this Agreement," but Exhibit B — the Mortgage Loan Schedule that identifies the loans, servicers and custodians — is attached only as "Provided Upon Request." Incorporating an exhibit that contains nothing leaves the incorporated content to extrinsic proof.

The Assignments of Mortgage are said to be "subject to recordation," language that does not say whether recording is required or merely permitted, and the obligation crystallizes only if recordation is "necessary under applicable law or requested by the Purchaser." Exhibit A-1(e), by contrast, tells the Seller when the assignment "must be duly recorded."

The carve-out reads "so long as such promotional material either is sent to the mortgagors for all of the mortgages in the servicing portfolio ...", where the "either" has no matching "or" and the alternative has dropped out. What kinds of mailings are permitted cannot be read from the sentence.

This paragraph exempts promotions "directed to the general public at large (including, without limitation, mass mailing based on commercially acquired mailing lists)," while clause (i) of the preceding paragraph permits mailings only if they do not "specifically target Mortgagors" and go to the whole servicing portfolio. A mass mailing from a purchased list can satisfy one and not the other.

The agreement is "deemed in effect when a fully executed counterpart thereof is received by the Purchaser in the State of New York," which sits against its being "dated as of May 1, 2007" and Subsection 6.01's conveyance "simultaneously with the execution and delivery of this Agreement." When the sale took effect is not fixed by the instrument.

Exhibit A-1 says the Mortgage Loan Documents "shall be delivered to the Purchaser, or to such other Person as the Purchaser shall designate," while Subsection 6.03 — the provision it cites — requires only that the Custodians certify what they hold and continue holding the documents for the Purchaser. Whether the Seller had to deliver the original notes and mortgages at all cannot be squared between them.

This exhibit qualifies the Mortgage File items "(to the extent in the possession of the applicable Seller)," while the "Mortgage File" definition qualifies the same Exhibit A-2 list "(to the extent in the possession of the applicable Servicer)." Whose possession measures the delivery obligation is unresolved.

The Assignor assigns the Purchase Agreements "except as described below," and the reservation that follows carves out only loans not on the Mortgage Loan Schedule — it does not carry the Subsection 6.01 exclusion of the Group 1 Mortgage Loans from the assignment of the Prior Purchase Agreements. Whether the Group 1 originator warranties were assigned turns on that mismatch.

The Assignor warrants that "[a]ttached hereto as Exhibit B are true and accurate copies of the Purchase Agreements," but Exhibit B to the form as attached is a blank page bearing only the heading "Purchase Agreements." What was warranted as attached cannot be identified from the document.

The Assignor warrants that Exhibit C contains "true and accurate copies of the Servicing Agreements," but Exhibit C to the form as attached is a blank page bearing only that heading. The subject matter of the warranty is not in the instrument.

The sentence says "No consent ... is required for the transactions ... having jurisdiction over the Assignor is required or, if required ...", repeating "is required" and leaving the representation ungrammatical. It also conditions obtaining consents on "the Closing Date," a term this Assignment Agreement does not define.

The Assignor represents that no third-party consent is needed to assign its rights "in the Agreements," a capitalized term this Assignment Agreement never defines — it defines "Purchase Agreements" and "Servicing Agreements" separately. What the representation covers is therefore uncertain.

This clause makes the Assignment Agreement control over "any provision of the Purchase Agreements or the Servicing Agreements with respect to the Mortgage Loans," although the whole point of the assignment is to pass the Originators' warranties and remedies under those agreements through to the Assignee. How far the short assignment displaces the underlying agreements' terms is unresolved.

The warranty is qualified "Except as set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule," but the Mortgage Loan Schedule definition lists no delinquency or exception field in which such items could be set forth. The carve-out has no ascertainable content.

Coverage must be from "a generally acceptable insurer," against hazards "customarily insured against in the jurisdiction" and "acceptable to the Rating Agencies," none of which is defined or measured. Whether a given policy satisfies the warranty cannot be determined from the text.

The representation covers "[a]ny and all requirements of any federal, state or local law" with an open-ended "including, without limitation" list, so the enumerated statutes give the residual no boundary. Its reach beyond lending-specific law is undetermined.

The list of permitted liens is defective on its face: item (2) has lost its text, leaving only the word "payable;" where the current-taxes exception should be, and the enumeration then jumps to (3). Which encumbrances the lien warranty tolerates cannot be read from the provision.

The documents are warranted to "have been duly and properly executed by other such related parties," an evident error for "such related parties," so as written the warranty speaks of parties other than those identified. The scope of the execution warranty turns on the mistake.

The title policy is warranted subject only to "the exceptions contained in clauses (1), (2) and (3) of paragraph (e) of this Exhibit F," but this Exhibit F has no paragraph (e); the lien exceptions are in paragraph (E), whose clause (2) is itself missing its text. The permitted exceptions cannot be identified from the cross-reference.

The no-defaults warranty is qualified "[e]xcept as set forth in paragraph (b) above," but paragraph (B) of this Exhibit is the No Defenses representation; the payment-history exceptions are in paragraph (A). The cross-reference points to the wrong warranty.

The Mortgage is warranted to contain "customary and enforceable provisions such as to render the rights and remedies of the holder thereof adequate" for realization, with no benchmark for what is customary or adequate. Whether a particular mortgage form breaches it is left at large.

The due-on-sale warranty is given only "[w]ith respect to each Fixed Rate Mortgage Loan," leaving the adjustable-rate loans in the pool outside it. Whether that omission is deliberate expressio unius or a gap is unaddressed.

The sentence reads "The Mortgaged Property is undamaged by waste, fire, adversely the value of the Mortgaged Property as security," with the list of casualties and the connecting words dropped out. What condition of the property is warranted cannot be read from the text.

The warranty turns on the borrower's not qualifying "taking into such facts as, without limitation," his credit history and ratios — a phrase missing the word "account" and with an open-ended list. What the originator had to weigh, and against what standard, is indeterminate.

"No Mortgage Loan is a High Cost Loan or Covered Loan, as applicable" leaves "as applicable" undefined, so it is unclear whether the warranty is absolute or limited to jurisdictions where those categories exist. This is one of the clauses that Subsection 8.02 deems material if breached, so the qualifier matters.

The warranty requires modifications to have been "approved by the issuer of the title insurer," a garbled phrase leaving whose approval was needed unclear, and requires modification terms to be "reflected in the Mortgage Loan Schedule," which has no such field. Neither requirement can be applied as written.

The appraisal must be by a Qualified Appraiser "duly appointed by the Seller," although the recitals state the Seller bought these loans from Originators who obtained the appraisals at origination. The requirement cannot be met on its own terms for purchased loans.

The warranty turns on "LTV," which is not a defined term in this agreement — Section 1 defines "Loan-to-Value Ratio" and "CLTV" as different measures. Whether second-lien loans are tested by the combined ratio or only by the second lien balance is left open.

The Seller warrants that each prepayment penalty "will be enforced by the Seller for the benefit of the Purchaser," although the loans are sold servicing-retained under Servicing Agreements assigned to the Purchaser and collection lies with the Servicers. Who must enforce, and what breach follows from non-collection, cannot be squared with Section 7.

The Schedule is warranted "complete, true and correct as of the Cut-off Date" of June 1, 2007, but Subsection 8.02 makes the Part B warranties as of the May 31, 2007 Closing Date — a date before the one the warranty speaks to. The two dates cannot be worked together.

This Part B ownership warranty is given as to every Mortgage Loan and duplicates Part A(S), which is given only for Group 1 Mortgage Loans, leaving the Part A/Part B division without consistent effect. That division controls which breaches are deemed material under Subsection 8.02.

The compliance warranty reaches "[a]ny and all requirements of any federal, state or local law" with an unbounded "including, without limitation" list. How far past the enumerated lending statutes the residual carries is unresolved.

The loans are warranted to "conform to the securitization requirements and loan level representations and warranties that are consistent with those applicable to a securitization transaction" of a described general kind, a standard with no identified source document or criteria. Because Subsection 8.03 makes breach of this clause a repurchase trigger, its indeterminacy is consequential.

The sentence states that none of "the above ratings" has been lowered, qualified or withdrawn, but it appears in a schedule whose table is garbled — the Class B-3 line shows "Baa3" with "BBB-" detached below the sentence — and it does not say who makes the statement or with what effect. Whether it is a representation by anyone, and as of what date, is unclear.
